utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, everybody. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Case Number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam. Mr. Brdjanin, can you follow the proceeding in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And good morning to you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Julian Nicholls with Joanna Korner and Denise Gustin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And good morning to you all. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman with David Cunningham and Aleksandar Vujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you. And welcome back. Today we have a new witness. But before we start with the new witness, do you have anything to tell us, Mr. Ackerman? First of all, how are you feeling?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm feeling much better. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't know if I have anything else to tell you. You're hinting at something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm concerned at the possibility of going beyond the end of January to finish your case, and of course if you need to finish in more -- more days to finish your case beyond the end of January, it's not going to be a major confrontation, major battle with us, provided it doesn't go on and on and on. So what's the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the current date, assuming every witness comes and takes the amount of time that we've predicted is -- February 12th would be our last sitting day. I think we'll finish quicker than that because I think some of those witnesses won't come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then if that would be the case, I would like to know whether you would still require -- anyway, but I prefer not to waste time -- not to use the sitting time to discuss that. If necessary, we'll have a short meeting on that, and that's the time you need for preparing the closing statements and whatever. We go through the plan again once more, but it can be done later without taking our time here. The witnesses for this week, we have number 33 starting today, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you anticipate will last with cross-examination -- do you anticipate a long detailed cross-examination, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I hope it's going to be short, but I don't know yet. Probably a couple hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How many witnesses do you have laid out for this week?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me look, Your Honour. We have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because on paper I have three.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: One, two, three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On paper, I have three.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's what we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You plan to have the first two between today and Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The second witness will be available to testify on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But then what about the -- yeah, Mr. Cunningham informed us of that. And the third one was scheduled to require two days of testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The third one is coming in at the same time, Your Honour, and will be available as soon as we finish the second one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but the second one was scheduled to last a day and a half at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that may happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And which --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The third one may have to remain over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Provided you understand that and he's prepared for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's a possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But please do put that witness in the picture straight away because I don't want long faces and witnesses do get tired.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Especially when it starts heating up, as I can see this past three.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I was listening while I was ill to the proceedings, Your Honour, and I recall a time when Ms. Korner complained that we were having down time, and she said it would be better to have witnesses stacked up waiting than have down time. That's expensive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On the other hand, Mr. Ackerman, I would rather prefer to have a witness stay here the weekend rather than find ourselves with nothing to do on a Friday. That is also very expensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I was trying to avoid that, Your Honour, because earlier complaints that were directed, I guess to you, that we were keeping witnesses here too long --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's true, and the complaints are still there, but we are approaching the end and I think it will be false economy if we tried to work out otherwise. I don't know anyway. I mean, if it's problematic for you or for the Tribunal structure, then let me know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I reworked the list last week, and I'm really compressing people pretty tightly now. So I think we're going to have people sitting here rather than people not being here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's my opinion. That's why I agreed with Ms. Korner's suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: One of the reasons, just so the Chamber will understand that it might make sense to keep people over the weekend now and then is because of the -- it's that season in Serbia and Republika Srpska where everybody has their what they call Slavas, it's their saint days. So they all bunch up right in November and December. So a lot of these people are doing these huge celebrations on Saturdays, and won't travel on Saturdays, and can only come on Sundays.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know enough about it anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that's the problem. We've run into it two or three times now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just make one inquiry about the timetable. Can we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher. Any preliminaries before we bring in the...? Usher, could you escort the witness into the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There was one matter that we need to go back to private session for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then let's go back to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Also, we didn't hear anything, and of course being a Defence witness, and the system being what it is, I was very reluctant to ask any questions about the offices themselves or the premises themselves because when she gave evidence, she gave information on that, and we didn't hear anything from the other witness. Anyway, it --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: For the moment, let's just wait and then I'll see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's see who the next witness is. There are no protective measures in place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're about to give evidence, testimony, and our rules require that before you do so, you enter a solemn declaration, something similar and equivalent, as far as legal effects are concerned, to an oath in several jurisdictions that in the course of your testimony, you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text of the solemn declaration is being handed to you now. Please read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please take a chair. So Mr. Vidic, let me explain to you very briefly what's going to happen. You're going to give evidence now, and since you are a witness called by the Defence, a Defence witness, the first series of questions that will be put to you will be coming from the lawyers representing Mr. Brdjanin, who is the accused in this case. After that, you will be cross-examined. In other words, you will be asked questions by Mr. Nicholls, I suppose, Mr. Nicholls, who is appearing for the Prosecution today. And you realise that there are two sides, the Prosecution and the Defence, and you are a witness for the Defence. Doesn't mean to say that you're here to favour the Defence or that you have a right to discriminate between the Defence and the Prosecution. Your obligation under the undertaking -- solemn undertaking that you have taken with us, made with us, is that you speak the truth and you answer each question as fully and as truthfully as possible, irrespective of who is putting the question to you. In other words, whether it's coming from the Prosecution or from the Defence, the requirement is that you answer truthfully each time. This is an advice that I give to every witness that comes here. And the second advice is don't try to go around in circles or give more information than you are asked for. Please, in answering the questions that are put to you, answer the question, the whole question, and nothing but the question. And that ensures that you will be out of this courtroom the earliest possible. Otherwise, you will be here for days, and I am sure that everyone will get fed up, and probably foremost yourself. Okay? Did I make myself understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman or Mr. Cunningham? Mr. Ackerman, who is the lead counsel for Mr. Brdjanin will be examining you in chief. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Your Honour, as has become our practice, I have prepared a book of exhibits for the witness, and I'll ask the usher to deliver it to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I don't have, Mr. Ackerman, and that's because everything arrived late, is a summary of the witness's proposed testimony. You don't have it either? I don't think either of us... Do you have it, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We got it, I think, late on Thursday or Thursday morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I sincerely apologise. I thought it had been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I could understand that it could also be somewhere, because the list of documents arrived this morning, and my secretary was preparing everything this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I thought it had been emailed to you in the normal course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It may well be, but everything was done this morning. So yes, Mr. Ackerman, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your name is Dobrivoje Vidic?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And where do you live, Mr. Vidic?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: At the moment in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you tell the Chamber just briefly about your educational background and your highest level of education that you've attained?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: I'm an architect by profession. I own a private company. Many engineers are involved. We are a stock company. We are working on public projects, and I'm also into urban planning. I plan towns and physical space in general, entire areas and regions, their infrastructure, and so on and so forth. I completed my studies in Belgrade in the 1980s. I was always involved in my profession. Well, most of the time, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Where were you living in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: 1991, 1992, I resided in a small village 50 kilometres from Banja Luka. The name of the village is Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In -- during that period of time, and especially directing your attention to 1991, did you become involved in politics with the advent of the multiparty elections that were going to be held in that period of time?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you join any particular political party?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. The free democratic elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina took place in 1990, in late 1990. I had a personal need to get involved in politics. My greatest reason for doing so was my desire, the ideal that I held. My understanding was that it was necessary to introduce democracy and institutions of democracy in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Through my work, through my profession, I was particularly involved with an area of activity called urban planning. This area deals with urban infrastructure in towns and entire countries. This is an area of study well known throughout the world. It was early on that I noticed that our system at the time in the socialist Yugoslavia was not like the system that was common at the time in the world. I became very interested. And this, in a manner of speaking, got me involved in politics. I started studying the kind of literature favouring a liberal and democratic society. I tried to obtain the right books. I tried to attend international conferences and obtain the kind of literature that was advocating democracy. At one point I decided I should make a personal contribution to this process, and in 1992, when I think back, perhaps a little naively, before I even became actively involved in trying to set up a political party, I started making plans for new environment, some sort of civilian society. That was my main subject of study. In 1990, at least to the extent that I can still remember, my main envisaged aim was to change society itself, to introduce democratic institutions. Frankly, my friends and other people I knew were more than anything frustrated by fear, frustrated by division along ethnic lines, because the Bosnian society at the moment, the society in Bosnia and Herzegovina, under its constitution was established as a state where power was divided between the different ethnic groups. The institutions of civil society were not functioning properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you've gone a little beyond the question, "Did you join a particular political party?" Your answer was that you did and then you explained to us some of the background of your interest in politics and why you got interested in politics. And -- just a minute, don't answer until I ask you a question. Then I think what you were trying to do was to tell us about what was happening politically in 1990 in Bosnia that started causing you and others that you knew some concern. And I think that's important, so please tell us what you were observing during that time that caused you to have some concern and to feel like you should get involved in politics. What was it you were seeing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps you can start by telling us how old you were at the time. It seems you are about in your late 40s now, no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm 50. In fact, it is my birthday today. So in 1990 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Happy birthday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So in 1990, that was -- well, I can't really figure it out. I would be 40, in fact, 38 or 39.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, so now perhaps you can answer Mr. Ackerman's question. So please tell us what you were observing during that time caused you to have some concern and to feel like you should get involved in politics. What was it you were seeing happening around you? That was your question -- or rather, the question that was put. And try to be as concise as possible, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Citizens were mostly frustrated. They felt that democracy should put them in their own ethnic groups. That was the heritage of the former system. The only important thing it was felt was that politically you should approach your own ethnic group. Through politics, I tried to make my contribution to democracy, but the real problem was that I did not have the money. I did not have the possibility to form my own party. Since the processes were going really fast --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me. We have interpreters who are desperately trying to keep up you with and failing, I think. So please speak a little bit slower and give them a chance to do their job. Because they're really good, but they can't go as fast as you can.

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: After I became active in mid-1990, I was thinking that perhaps I could form some kind of a local association which would be affiliated to a strong political party which had influence throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina. At that time, on the political scene, there were some strong parties which were strongly polarised. They each had their own ethnic group behind them, SDA, HDZ, and SDS. The opposition that remained was the thinkers from the former regime, socialists who, according to my mind, had highly conservative ideas, and they used democracy, or rather the elections, to prevent change. So my options were quite limited as to whom I should join if I wanted to become active in politics. I decided, therefore, to join the SDS in 1990, in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Now, after -- by the way, I think this is about the third or fourth witness who we have had here on their birthday, Your Honours, which probably defies all the odds that we could figure on that. So happy birthday. After you joined the SDS, did you hold any positions within that party during the time you were a member?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, no. I did not have any functions until the end of the elections. After that, I became the deputy in -- deputy in the assembly. I'm not quite sure now whether I was in any kind of a commission or on any kind of board. But right at the beginning, before the elections, there were some political misunderstandings or conflicts already.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you become a member of the main board of the SDS at any point?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it happened the next year after the elections, in 1991. At a session to mark the anniversary of some kind, if I recall correctly, it was in July 1991. I was appointed to a body of the main board, although in February, this means after the elections, after I was elected as a deputy to the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I had a conflict with the SDS politicians at the local level. I did not agree with their policy, and I was thrown out of all the bodies at the municipal level, in the municipality where I lived. But the party was keen on keeping me as a deputy because I was elected as such to the assembly, and that is why the party tried to get me involved in their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How long did you remain a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: From July 1990 until February 1991, or perhaps it was March. That is when, at the session of the SDS in the Municipality of Prnjavor, I was dismissed from all my functions. However, I continued to be a deputy in the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And then I was appointed to the main board of the SDS, and I attended many meetings in this capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So are you still a member of the SDS today?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When did you officially end your membership in that party?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: There are some periods in which I was strongly opposed or when my views were very much different from their views. It was in February 1991, and then in December, January, or February of 1992. And in February or March of 1992, I did not attend the sessions of the main board at all and also, the sessions of the assembly until the fall of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I still need to have an answer to the question of when you ended your membership in SDS. Do you remember approximately what date you stopped being a member?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: The party did not operate in such a way that you could say I'm no longer a member of the party. At one point, you were admitted to the party, you became a member. And it was up to you to decide when to leave. The act of dismissal was not official, but it was quite clear that I was treated as a dissident by the entire party. I was treated that way all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we need to know exactly when this happened. I mean, it's -- in other areas where I am familiar with, you cease to be a member of a party or of an association when you signify the termination of your membership, either by not paying any more and writing saying that "I'm ceasing -- stopping my membership now." I mean, it's not automatic; it doesn't happen just like that. In fact, if you don't usually write a letter to that effect or inform them officially that you're ceasing from being a member, they would still send you -- you would still be responsible for the payment of the annual membership fee, et cetera, et cetera. But we need to know. The whole purpose of Mr. Ackerman's question was to place this within a time frame so that we know exactly when you ceased to have any connections with the SDS, particularly as with regard to your being a member of the party.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not pay the membership fee in the SDS ever. But I did not join any other party until 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you resign your membership? I mean, did you send a letter to the SDS saying, "I am no longer a member." Never? So on what basis do you maintain that you are not a member of the SDS now? Because if there was never any membership being paid. How do you become a member and how do you cease to become a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You signed an admission form for the admission to the party, and you also took part in some meetings and things like that. But the very act of dismissal -- officially, I was thrown out of all my functions in February or March in 1991. But as a member and as a citizen, you would not be thrown out of the party. This was not how it was done. I never submitted any kind of a written letter to the party indicating that I was no longer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Is it that important for you? Let's move ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think I understand. I'll ask one more clarifying question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There came a time when you absolutely ceased participating in any activities of the SDS. I think that's what you told us. Could you tell us about when that was, that you ceased SDS activity.

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: I have to admit that it happened on several occasions. I would stop, and then I would come back. The first time when I no longer attended the meetings, I was no longer an active member, I simply withdrew, that was in 1992 in February -- January or February.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I want to talk to you about regionalisation and ask you if you had any interest in regionalisation. I think you know what I'm talking about when you say regionalisation. Did you have any interest in that process?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And could you tell the Chamber what it was that caused you to become interested in regionalisation and what that interest entailed.

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: While I was a deputy in the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I noticed that the assembly could not function properly because people were trying to outvote each other. The political parties in Bosnia and Herzegovina were there to express solely ethnic affiliation, and there was very little interest in the -- in obtaining real changes in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the civil society there. I felt that my region was in a very real danger. I will now try to explain to you what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you do that, when you explain that, try to explain it as briefly and as concisely as you can. What was the danger that you believed your region was in? What was that danger?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina was not a state with democratic institutions. The only thing that was there was the elections. It was a republic which had a great deal of autonomy in Yugoslavia. It was like a company that owned all its property, all its assets. It was not like in democratic states where there were real owners of the property, which meant that the state had owned all the factories, all the companies, and had a great deal of power that way. There was a danger that if the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina was not regionalised with the kind of outvoting that was going on in the assembly - we also have to know that the central government had much more power than in normal democratic countries - I believe that there was a danger at the time that the funds would be moved from one region to another. My political idea was to launch the process of regionalisation of certain areas. I was particularly interested in achieving the regionalisation of the area where I lived. It was a developed part of the country with a developed agriculture. And since in the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there was a long, long debate which always ended in attempts to win majority by outvoting on the part of one ethnic group over another, they were all trying to achieve the power to rule, to control the assets of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was the essence of what they were trying to achieve, not democracy. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So because of this concern that you saw the events that you saw happening in that regard, you became concerned, did you, about your region? And I take it that would be the Krajina region. And what was it you were afraid would happen in the Krajina region that got you concerned?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: There were some key issues. One issue, for instance, was the property of the state-owned companies. It was in all the towns, so the local government would appoint directors of such companies, and through them it would control the property. I think that you can all see what the possible consequences are. The second type of danger was to the safety of the inhabitants. The events in Croatia were quite frustrating for the public and caused a great deal of concern and fear because there was this horrible, dirty war there. Many people simply wanted to feel safe. In the end, it turned out that the fear was justified because those who took the functions, positions in the state, was in a position to actually endanger certain areas and regions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So based upon all of that, what, if anything, did you do regarding regionalisation, you personally?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. My idea was to try on a voluntary basis to find people, like-minded people, and then that we would put forward first the proposal for an association of municipalities, and then to establish a multiethnic region which would first set up a legitimate body which could be established by appointing the deputies who had already been elected from all ethnic groups in the region. And then we would launch negotiations, diplomatic negotiations with the government and the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina which, at that time, had already violated certain protective institutions, protective instruments that existed in the constitution. The government and the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina violated the constitution and its own rules of procedure. That was the idea I had, to do things on a diplomatic field, to negotiate with the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina through a legitimate body which would represent all the citizens in order for the work of that body not to be in violation of certain international rules. In particular, the charter on civil and political liberties.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So the idea was a multiethnic association designed to protect the economic interests of the people in the Krajina. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And did you make -- did you take any steps, then, to form that organisation? Were steps taken? Were you part of it?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: I first talked to my colleagues, deputies in the assembly, some friends of mine, and also some people from other parties, and I got quite a lot of support for this idea. A group was established following this initiative of mine, but I have to admit that I did not have that much influence in the SDS. I simply had to talk and try to persuade a certain small number of people. But when you get things on a higher level, then things either changed and things were done in a different way, and the goal that I wanted to achieve was not achieved. If at the beginning the idea was to establish an association of municipalities, the association of municipalities was not supposed to be any kind of authority, did not have to have its own government or anything. The idea was to unite the municipalities and to aid them to achieve some kind of an agreement so that they can then protect their interests, those interests that they all had in common. The organisation itself was based on the provisions of the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Now, if you will look in your book at Exhibit P160, 1-6-0, that's it. You have it right in front of you. That's it. It's a press report that deals with the formation of the Association of Bosanska Krajina Municipalities on 27 April 1991. Were you involved in that process? Were you at that meeting? Were you involved in the creation of this association on 26 April, 1991?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And so this association actually got formed on that date, did it not?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the association that was formed on that date, was it formed - and you alluded to this just a moment ago - was it formed as a voluntary association or was it formed as a level of government?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: It was a voluntary organisation. It was the steering committee. It was just an initiative that was launched. At the first meeting, it was not clear yet. There was a bit of confusion. There were some people, some deputies who were opposed to this idea. It was supposed to be the first, initial meeting. There were some results. A representative of this association was elected.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look now at Exhibit P11, this is a report on the second session of this assembly of ZOBK, as it was called. If you look under item 3, I think you're going to find your name. And could you just explain to the Trial Chamber what that meeting was about and what you -- position you were elected to and what that position entailed, if you could?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: This is the first serious meeting at the cultural centre in Banja Luka with representatives of the municipalities in attendance. May I remind you, in every municipality, there were deputies at the local level, and each municipality sent one, two, or three of its representatives to this meeting. These representatives then helped to put together an initiative to establish an association of municipalities. At this meeting, there was a proposal and proclamation. Members were proposed to be appointed to the executive board, Andjelko Grahovac. That's when my name was put forward, too. I think it was Mr. Brdjanin, as a matter of fact, who put my name forward as vice-president of the executive board. I was supposed to be in charge of the economy, the economic activity, as far as I remember. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So what happened to your concept that you just explained to the Chamber of a multiethnic association that could represent the Krajina in negotiations with the republic? What happened to that idea? Did it get carried into effect in this organisation we're just talking about here or not?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Not at this precise moment, not at this meeting, nor later, at least not the way I imagined it should be done. However, at the very outset, I could not oppose this because any initiative to establish an association of municipalities would have been a good one. Also because this did not mean that any authorities would immediately be established. Therefore, I simply allowed myself to follow my own ideas. Throughout the work of the assembly, the idea was to set up a body that would decide on its own multiethnic nature and that deputies should come from all the parties, whereas here you had only the representatives of the municipalities. And it all depended on who the specific municipality would send to the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I take it there did come a time when it became clear to you that your -- that your ideas, that your dream was not going to be able to become a reality. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: That's true. The reason was that even this kind of organisation and association of municipalities was viciously attacked by people close to the top of the Serbian Democratic Party. This was a political platform in the Krajina or in the centre of Banja Luka, the centre of which was in Sarajevo. You knew exactly which the people were who were attacking or undermining this initiative, keeping anything from actually being established. Even the work of the municipality itself was under attack and did not enjoy adequate support from the top level of the SDS. This affected the organisation of our work, which after a while boiled down to convening sessions that were not even attended by a sufficient number of members. The approach became informal, and the association of municipalities was merely there to issue the occasional press release, make announcements every now and then. The real power, however, was exercised at municipality level. Municipalities throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina were different from what they were at the time in the democratic world. The municipalities in our society, as it was, were the first body under the state itself, directly subordinated to the state itself. They were not independent units as seems to be the tendency now. The municipalities each had their secretaries in charge of legal affairs who passed opinions on what was feasible and what was not. They worked under state laws mainly, the laws that Bosnia and Herzegovina had inherited. Throughout this period, the laws of Bosnia and Herzegovina were the ones that were enforced throughout the municipalities. Any decisions by this Krajina Municipality throughout this particular period of time were mostly of an advisory nature, the occasional press release, public announcements, that sort of thing. And in as far as was possible, these were then implemented occasionally at municipal level, wherever legally feasible. However, I know from my own experience that most of those decisions that were adopted under varying circumstances with no proper procedure in a way that was not even serious enough. You didn't even know what had been adopted. There were announcements made for the public in the newspapers, but the majority of those decisions were actually illegal [Realtime transcript read in error "legal"], and therefore the municipalities could not implement them. The assembly did not have a proper legal filter, so to speak, in order to be able to decide what was legally feasible and what wasn't. Anything could have been adopted because in essence there was not a single body that was there to enforce these decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll stop you there. There came a time when this association, ZOBK, transformed itself into the ARK, the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Were you still involved in that regional process when that happened? And I'm not asking you to look at a document. I just want to know if you were involved in --

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, I will ask you -- yeah, I thought so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just a moment. Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 25, line 21, the word right there at the beginning should be "illegal," not "legal."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 25, line 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He said: "The majority of those decisions were actually illegal, and therefore the municipalities could not implement them."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Before we go into the ARK, I mean, I'm going through this part of the evidence, where did the initiative to form the ZOBK come from? Where did it originate? Who took the first steps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure about this, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Especially when you have various municipalities coming together to form something like this, someone must have taken the initiative or inspired the whole.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly. Certain municipal circles were interested. There were conversations where this was discussed months ahead of time. It's very difficult to say precisely who provided the initiative. I know about my own ideas that I presented. Eventually, it happened naturally. I'm not sure, however, who was the one to provide the initiative. But I do know that the leaders of the SDS were not keen on that. You could clearly see that at the first session in Celinac when there was a heated argument. The people who were involved in this argument were later to become very successful members of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But would you agree that it was a Serbian initiative?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that moment, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In fact, earlier, I think you said you were one of the people who came up with the idea and started the discussion, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: I also tried to contribute to the establishment of the association of municipalities. My idea was to adopt a multiethnic approach. At the very outset, the association of municipalities was supposed to be as the municipalities themselves multiethnic. If their representatives were there, it could be considered that the Krajina itself was multiethnic. This was not government level yet. It was later that I thought a mini-parliamentary local body could be established that could then demand autonomy from the central government of Bosnia and Herzegovina through negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you first started discussing this, I think you said you discussed it with other members of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Did you discuss it with non-Serb members of that assembly from the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And did you receive support from any of those people for that concept?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: From some, but many in Sarajevo denied me their support. In Krajina itself, many were prepared to talk about it. A number of my friends approved of the idea of regionalisation and believed that this was feasible. However, my supporters as a rule were people who understood democracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, when you talk about your friends and your supporters, are you talking exclusively about Serb friends and supporters, or was that a multiethnic group of people?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: It is a multiethnic group. I had many friends in my political debates and negotiations who were not Serbs, who included both Croats and Muslims, and those were prominent intellectuals, people very much in the public eye. I can provide you with names if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to go now to the formation of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. And I want you to look at P80, which you have there in your book, P8-0, which is the statute of the autonomous region. And the first part I want to bring to your attention are the two articles, 10 and 11. Let me know when you've found those and had a chance to look at them. Now, those two articles, 10 and 11, what kind of an organisation are those articles describing? Are they describing an association, voluntary association, or are they describing a level of government?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: These two articles are describing the possibility of the municipalities joining an association on a voluntary basis only, or leaving [Realtime transcript read in error "leading"] the association on a voluntary basis. Furthermore, they state that any municipality may join the association. Article 10 states this very clearly. Within the Autonomous Region of Krajina, other municipalities may join. Here you have it, Article 11. Freedom of association for the municipalities within one calendar year.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Was any municipality required to be a member of the association? Or was any municipality prohibited from leaving the association, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They are two questions pooled together. You may answer yes or no to either of them, or if you want to separate them, you're free to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, page 29, line 9, the word is not "leading," but "leaving." "Leaving" instead of "leading."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you understand my question, or should we start over?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think separate the questions yourself, Mr. Ackerman, because it will be easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was any municipality ever required to be a member of the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: No. No municipality was ever required to be a member of the autonomous region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, let's move to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was any municipality ever prohibited from leaving the association if they had wanted to?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: No. No municipality was ever prohibited from leaving the association.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I now want to call your attention to Article 35 of the statute. And the second paragraph of Article 35 says: "Decisions and conclusions of the Assembly shall become binding for the associated municipalities once they have been approved by the Assemblies of Municipalities." Now, as a member of this association representing Prnjavor, what was your understanding of the meaning of that paragraph? How did that apply to your municipality of Prnjavor, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Paragraph stating that the municipalities must apply these, the municipalities could not apply anything that was not legal. The municipalities would assume the responsibility to implement any of the decisions. For example, if a municipality which was the case all the time, so to speak, decisions were not implemented in any of the municipalities. Very often, they were confusing, awkwardly put together. They did not reflect the common interests. Therefore, the municipalities did not implement those. Krajina did not have the instruments of power to dissolve the assembly or to subordinate it in any legal way. Only the central republic government of Bosnia and Herzegovina had the power to do that. There was no legal or physical instrument for them to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. The next document that I want you to look at is P95. And P95 is the 10th session of the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina held in Banja Luka. And if you notice on the first page in the agenda section, it indicates that part of the agenda is a report by you on the work of the government of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. But before we get to that, I would like to draw your attention to a couple of paragraphs under item 2. There is a report from the Banja Luka Security Services Centre and a report from representatives of the JNA on one Veljko Milankovic and his arrest. Were you familiar with that at the time that it occurred, the arrest of Milankovic?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if you go, then, to the next -- I think it's maybe on the next page, it's when you give your report. Apparently during the giving of your report, you mention a personal issue apparently that you had with Mr. Milankovic when you apparently told the assembly that he even drew a weapon on you as president of the SDS, a member of the BH Assembly, and vice-chairman of the executive council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which part of Exhibit P95 are you referring to, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm on page 2. It's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think page 2 may be missing from the exhibit which has been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't know how it could be missing. It's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not missing on the screen. Unfortunately what we have here, Mr. Ackerman, is -- my -- at least, my P95, is I have page 1, and then at the back, there should be page 2, but there is page 3. So page 2 is missing. That is what -- so, Madam Registrar --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We should probably check the original record and see if it's complete or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what we need to do anyway. Anyway, please proceed, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Was that the case, was that a report that you actually made about your run-in with Mr. Milankovic?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you describe that a little bit, in a little more detail to the Chamber? Did you actually have such a -- what happened? What was that situation?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: At that time, the frustration was great. There was a war in neighbouring Croatia and paramilitary units started showing up in the area. There was a great danger that the different groups would identify themselves with the assembly of the Krajina and with this association of municipalities. There were people walking around informally bringing with them armed persons. I was not particularly active in the work of the executive council as the president was, and the rest of them. But as the association of municipalities itself was in disorder, which you can clearly see from this report. The president of the association of municipalities convened this meeting in an ill-prepared manner. There was a lot of confusion. I was invited, and I had never been invited to any of their private meetings before, although at the first meeting it was decided that I would be professionally and gainfully employed, this was never carried out. Four or five months went by. I was gainfully employed with the municipality, but I did not attend too many of those meetings, and the assembly functioned very poorly. However, I did discuss the various dangers, what might happen. I discussed this with the president, and he convened a meeting of the assembly. I'm afraid there weren't sufficient people to have one to begin with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is nonresponsive, unless I'm really missing where he's going.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're not. I was just getting ready to interrupt him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Maybe you didn't understand my question. My question was: Could you just describe very briefly your encounter with Mr. Milankovic. What was that about? How did that happen when he pulled a gun on you?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milankovic had with him a grouped of armed persons who were just going about talking about the people, and they became very dangerous at one point. They were very often in the Krajina region, and they had brought with them journalists who took photos of them representing them to be the army, the official army of the Krajina. This was absolutely impermissible, and someone had to say something. I happened to know that man. I tried to reason with him, telling him this was no way to do it, telling him there were legal police bodies, the army, the Army of Yugoslavia. However, in one such conversation, he threatened me with the use of firearms. And that's why I summed up the courage to go to the meeting of the assembly, although I myself was not sure about suggesting this to the municipalities. The municipalities had their own police, but the assembly of the Krajina did not have any bodies that were directly subordinated to it. You needed to have consensus from the municipalities. You needed to have agreement at a higher level for this to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a 25-minute break now. Then we will stop shortly before noon. I explained last week that we have a swearing-in ceremony of the new Dutch ad litem judge, and I need to be there. That would replace the break we usually have at 12.30. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vidic, we're going to proceed. Mr. Vidic, I once more would like to emphasise the importance that you try and keep your answers strictly to the questions that are put to you and to be as concise as possible. Otherwise, you're going to be here the rest of the week. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Vidic, we're looking at Exhibit P95.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the understanding, Mr. Ackerman, you know that I don't like to stop the witnesses. I try to avoid it as much as you can. But I think we have discussed this a little bit. I wouldn't like to take you by surprise if I do between now and the end of the day because I think it's a bit necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Not a problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look under the conclusions of P95, first paragraph 2 and then paragraph 3, paragraph 2 indicates that there was a discussion followed by a conclusion regarding paramilitary formations. And the assembly is expressing its position basically that it is -- does not support paramilitary formations and that any military organisation should be under the control of the JNA at that point in time. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then finally in paragraph 3, there is a conclusion that probably followed a discussion regarding the arrest of Milankovic. In fact, it says that there was a lengthy debate and says the Autonomous Region of Krajina fully accepted the report and supported the measures and activities of the security organs of the JNA 5th Corps and the Banja Luka Security Services Centre. I take it that means --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like him to just ask the witness what the witness thinks it means rather than --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's fine. He's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What was the position that the autonomous region was taking regarding the arrest of Milankovic? Were they in favour of it or opposed?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: They were in favour of his arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, it says that that conclusion was arrived at after a lengthy debate. Do you remember what if anything Mr. Brdjanin had to say about the arrest of Milankovic and his feelings about it?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: I think that he agreed with the arrest and that such formations could not exist within the Krajina. So I think he was in favour. He agreed with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you hear him speak in that regard at this particular meeting, or did you hear him or read about his position in that regard from other places?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: He took an active part even in the arguments with the people who were leading those armed people. Mr. Brdjanin, in fact, took the most active role in bringing about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: "This" what?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Bringing about this what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Bringing about what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The things that are stated in the conclusions. In other words, that the paramilitary formation should be disarmed by the authorities and should be placed under the proper control.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I'm finished with that document now. And I'll simply ask you this: During the year 1992, were the municipalities of the Autonomous Region of Krajina bound in any way to implement the decisions of the ARK Assembly? Were they required to do so?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: During -- during 1992 between basically May and July, were the municipalities of the autonomous region bound or required to implement decisions and conclusions of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: In that period, the constitution and the laws were passed by the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the municipalities were bound to comply with the laws. There was the Official Gazette, and they all had to comply with this. There were also the instructions on how to work and how the crisis staffs in the municipalities were to be established, if there was any danger. The legal documents quite clearly indicate that the Crisis Staff of Krajina was an illegal body as far as I understood it. And I think that the municipalities acted accordingly. They had their own crisis staffs which were based on the appropriate laws. They also applied the existing laws of Bosnia and Herzegovina which provided for the establishment of crisis staffs at the municipal level.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not sure you answered my question. And let me ask it again, and please listen very carefully. Between May and July of 1992, were the municipalities of the autonomous region bound or required to implement decisions and conclusions of the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure because I do know that some municipalities did not implement that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were the police required or bound to implement decisions and conclusions of either the ARK Assembly or the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: No. The police was part of the ministry, and they abided by the chain of command that existed in the ministry. Responsibilities -- in terms of responsibilities, implementation, and the chain of command in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, page 38, line 12, I'm told that the witness said not "some municipalities," but "many municipalities" did not implement that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, I would like for the whole question and answer to be given again properly. I'm not happy, not for that respect, but for something else. I don't think that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question -- Mr. Vidic, I'm referring you back to a question that Mr. Ackerman put to you, which was the following: "I'm not sure you answered my question, and let me ask it again and please listen very carefully. Between May and July of 1992, were the municipalities of the autonomous region bound or required to implement decisions and conclusions of the ARK Crisis Staff?" And you answered: "I am not sure because I do know that some municipalities did not implement that." Now, the first point is it's being suggested that you didn't say "some municipalities," but you said "many municipalities did not implement that."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is my objection to some of these so-called corrections. I would like to have the whole question please asked again and the witness to give his answer without any prompting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So what is your answer to the question? Were the municipalities of the ARK bound or required to implement decisions and conclusions of the ARK Crisis Staff? What is your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to make a comment, and I apologise for that. I am not sure whether Krajina had the instruments of government whereby it could operate or act in the municipalities through these authorities. And pursuant to the constitution and the laws that were passed, it followed that Krajina could not force the municipalities to implement its decisions. Because the municipalities had the executive government, and Krajina did not have the executive government. This is what I base my conclusion on. And what I know, that many municipalities did not implement these decisions, and they did not -- no sanctions were imposed on them for this reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. You have explained about the Krajina and its nonexecutive powers. But the question that Mr. Ackerman had put to you in the first place referred to the Crisis Staff of the ARK and whether in your opinion, having lived those days, whether the municipalities were bound to follow, to observe the decisions taken by the crisis staff. That was the question. And what you have given us is an answer to some other question that was not put to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The situation was similar with the crisis staffs. As far as I know and as far as I can remember, because it was a long time ago, the Crisis Staff of Krajina, it seems to me - I'm not sure - but I can say that there was a certain duplication. I'm not sure. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Was the army bound to implement decisions and conclusions of either the ARK Assembly or the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think it would be better to break that up into two questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think you're right, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Was the army bound to implement decisions or conclusions of the ARK Assembly?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Was the army bound to implement decisions or conclusions of the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were you aware that Radoslav Brdjanin was the president of the ARK Crisis Staff? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know of anyone who was bound to follow the orders or instructions of Radoslav Brdjanin? Was there anyone to whom he was a superior that you knew of?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Vidic, thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, I think you need to start here because otherwise it doesn't make sense.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I apologise to you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me begin by asking you, sir, when were you first contacted by Mr. Brdjanin's Defence team about being a witness in this case?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: I don't know when it was exactly, but perhaps two or three months ago. Well, there was a contact about a year ago. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Who made the contact about a year ago?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this may be interesting, but I have no idea why this is relevant, who contacted him, when he was first contacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can't discount it as irrelevant straight away, Mr. Ackerman. I'll wait and see what the answer and what the next question would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I can say the reason is, Your Honour, that we have found out that statements have been taken in the past and that some witnesses have talked earlier. We've gotten these witness summaries very late. Not everything in this witness summary was covered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Nicholls. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me do this, as an officer of Court and an officer of this Chamber, I will never withhold a witness statement. If a witness has given a witness statement, it'll be given to the Prosecution. So we're wasting time to ask this person if he gave a witness statement. He didn't or the Prosecution would have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, that's very interesting, but if you could just let me finish with my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm objecting to it, so it's up to the Judge whether you -- the Prosecutor finishes with his questions or not. I think we're wasting time and it's a fishing expedition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We probably are, Mr. Ackerman, but I think we'll get there quicker if we proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If he has some good-faith reason for his question, then I don't have any objection to it. But he's just on a fishing expedition, he's trying to find something. He doesn't have any suspicions there even.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When you were contacted a year ago, all I want to know is did you meet somebody in person and talk to them about this case, about what your testimony might be? Or over the phone?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: As for the testimony for Radoslav Brdjanin, there was no contact a year ago. It was about some other issues which have no relevance for this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What issues were those? Because you said it was a contact from the Defence team, from Mr. Brdjanin's team.

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: A year ago? A year ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, as for the Defence of Radoslav Brdjanin, it was not a year ago. It was -- I don't know exactly when it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Nicholls. One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think it's possible that he's confused and it's another Defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It could well be, but witnesses should not get confused when the question is pretty straightforward. I mean your very first question on cross-examination was: "Let me begin by asking you, sir, when were you first contacted by Mr. Brdjanin's Defence team about being a witness in this case?" And he answered: "I don't know when it was exactly, but perhaps two or three months ago. Well, there was a contact about a year ago. I'm not quite sure." So when you mention there was a contact a year about a year ago, you were mentioning it within the context of a question that was put to you referring specifically to contacts made by the Brdjanin Defence team. If you want to make corrections, to correct yourself, feel free to do so. No one is after your blood. Don't misunderstand me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there was a contact that had to do with other persons. But the name of Radoslav Brdjanin was not mentioned at that time, a year ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But was the contact made by anybody on the Defence team of Mr. Brdjanin? Who was the person who contacted you about a year ago? Was it a certain Mr. Peric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You see. You'll get there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it had to do with testimony in another case, for Krajisnik. I don't know. We had only one conversation about a year ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. It's not important for me anyway. I mean, it's... Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: At the beginning of your testimony, you told us how you became politically active in the early 1990s and began taking part -- well, you ended up having several different positions within the SDS and various assemblies. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Well, these were not functions. Until the elections, I was the president of the municipal board of the SDS. Immediately after the election, I no longer held that function. I was merely a deputy. Later on I was involved -- I became a member of the main board as a deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And my question is before all of that, were you involved in politics? Were you involved in politics as a younger man, in your 20s?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: No. As a young man, no. I was over 35 when I got active in politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the whole time when you began your political activities, are you saying that you - Mr. Ackerman called it a dream - that you were trying to build this pluralistic representative party in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, it soon became apparent to you that with the SDS in your municipality, Prnjavor, that was not an acceptable position. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Well, to a certain extent, yes. But there were conflicts related to some other issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, but one of the issues that was clear was that the SDS in Prnjavor did not envisage itself transforming into a pluralistic representative parties of all people. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to show you, please, P1785.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm distributing my list now, Your Honour. I wasn't sure when exactly this was going to start.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you have that document, sir, in your language?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, if you look at that first paragraph, the very first paragraph, it talks about how this municipality, which was 72 per cent Serb, 13 per cent Muslim, and then just a few Croats and others, had earlier on lived in harmony. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then it talks about how interethnic relations had deteriorated, and you spoke a little bit about that on direct. That's the fear and mistrust between ethnicities that you were talking about when Mr. Ackerman was questioning you. Is that right? Now, the next paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the transcript has not picked up your answer. You may need to speak up a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The last question was a very important question. This first paragraph is correct, is it, it talks about the interethnic tensions and mistrust which you discussed with Mr. Ackerman. Correct? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This second paragraph states: "The SDS won a majority of votes in the elections, but extremist tendencies predominate in the senior leadership of this party where there are insufficient educated and competent people. Among the Serbs, there is a tendency to divide into moderate, left-leaning and extreme. This division is deepening and is leading to a rift amongst the Serbs." Now, this document is dated the 15th of March 1992, after you were essentially kicked out of your position as president. Correct? You need to answer --

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So that paragraph is correct as well, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: To ask if a paragraph is correct asks him to affirm every word of that paragraph, and I object to it in that regard. If there's some part of that that the witness says is not correct, then he should be permitted to say so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's obvious. Perhaps you can rephrase your question in a sense that if there's anything in that paragraph that the witness doesn't agree or disagrees with, then he should state it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Everything I have read to you from this document, you have affirmed it and that's the truth, isn't it? What I have read out aloud to you from this document is correct. Isn't that right? You've already said that it is.

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Sir, what you told me, that was what my answer referred to. But I was not focussed on the text itself. I was merely listening to what you were saying, and I provided an answer to your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Everything -- I don't want to go through it again, but the questions I asked you, the statements I read to you were true statements. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If he hasn't focussed on the paragraph or contents of the paragraph, Mr. Nicholls, you have to go through it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Let's do this again. Read the first paragraph. You told me you had read it. Read it again, please, if you didn't read it. You told me you read it, I thought. But please read the first paragraph. Let me know when you're done reading it.

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: I'm finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, this paragraph is correct, is it not, that approximately 72 per cent of the population of Prnjavor were Serbs? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That percentage of the population and the remaining of the population prior to the multiparty elections and the breakdown lived in relative harmony and peace. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: That's a good question. I would even be inclined to say no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Wasn't Prnjavor known as "little Europe" because everybody got along so well?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, but there were often fights in the town itself, interethnic fights, fights between Muslims and Serbs. Prior to that, there were drastic cases like that, just before the election.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just before the election. But what you answered when I first started questioning you, that yes, traditionally in Prnjavor the different ethnicities had lived together in harmony and tolerance. Go back into the mid-1980s. You need to answer with your voice, sir. I see you nodding, but you need to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: So there was a period of harmony that was about two years before the election. But if we talk about two years before the election, it's still a long shot from saying that life was harmonious.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "The SDS, Serbian Democratic Party" - look at the second paragraph, please - "won a majority of votes in the elections." That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "But extremist tendencies predominate in the senior leadership of this party." That was true at that time, isn't it? You spoke about that even on direct examination.

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "Where there are insufficient educated and competent people" -- the rest of that sentence, that's true as well, isn't it? That was part of the problem with the SDS party in Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "Among the Serbs, there is a tendency to divide into moderate, left-leaning and extreme. This division is deepening and is leading to a rift amongst the Serbs." That's true as well, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "The fact that the leading core of the SDS is encumbered by incompetence and criminal activity (smuggling weapons, aid to the Serbs, and other acts through achieving citizens' rights) is a particular problem."
