That's true as well, isn't it, that there were members of the SDS involved in smuggling weapons at that time in Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Members, persons, people who were smuggling weapons, but you can't say that this was the case with the leaders of the party. Certain individuals, yes; party leaders, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Individual members of the SDS were involved in smuggling weapons?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure about that. I can't really say who specifically but...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Skip five paragraphs, if you could, go down to the sixth paragraph and I think you'll see your name in it, in the second sentence. Tell me when you've found that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the page numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's page 2 in your original.

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Tell me when you've found that section.

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We can move on, but the paragraph I'm interested in starts: "They" - still talking about the SDS throughout this section - "also espouse a struggle against the Muslims." That's the same paragraph you've got. Right? Is that the paragraph you're looking at?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's the one I'm looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The next statement -- the next sentence states: "The cadres in the party are Dragan Djuric, president and businessman, blinded politically by extremism, became president in a putsch replacing Dobrivoje Vidic, an architect politically inclined towards the Serbian Renewal Movement, highly irresponsible, both also a national representative involved in arms smuggling and the idealogue behind the military formation in Kremna." Is it true that it was Dragan Djuric who replaced you? You talked about being replaced earlier.

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: As far as you know, is this an accurate sentence?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's a giant ambiguity here, so I really object to a question about "is it an accurate sentence"? If you begin with those words, "highly irresponsible," those could either apply to Dragan Djuric or they could apply to Dobrivoje Vidic; it's difficult to tell. But I think it's totally ambiguous in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls. I just don't agree with your interpretation, Mr. Ackerman, but I won't say more to leave the witness free to answer the question. Mr. Vidic, I would like you to read carefully the first part of that paragraph starting with the words or from the words, "they also espoused a struggle against the Muslims." And you can end with the part "and the idealogue of the military formation in Kremna." Read it carefully, and then I have one or two questions to ask you so that we clear this up. When you have finished reading it, tell me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was Mr. Djuric an architect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I was the one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are the one. Now, how is Mr. Djuric described in this first sentence of this paragraph? How is he described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Blinded by extremism, became president, Djuric, that is, in a putsch replacing Dobrivoje Vidic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And how are you described in that paragraph, in that sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As politically inclined towards the SPO. This is not accurate. That was just propaganda for me, but I was not politically inclined that way. Highly irresponsible, also a national deputy involved in arms smuggling, and the mastermind behind the formation of a paramilitary formation in Kremna. This is not true. Veljko Milankovic, commander of a paramilitary formation, this is simply not true because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When the paragraph uses the words "highly irresponsible," it's referring to you, no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And also a national representative, it's referring to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the allegation accusation of involvement in arms smuggling is referring to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, here in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, and also being the mastermind or the idealogue behind the military formation in Kremna is also supposedly referring to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what it says, just that it's not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Are you happy now, Mr. Ackerman? Thank you. Mr. Nicholls, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Veljko Milankovic's paramilitary formation was in Vucak, if I'm pronouncing it correctly? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nicholls, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Veljko Milankovic's paramilitary formation was from Vucak, isn't that right? They were called the Wolves from Vucak?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So you don't agree about some of the accusations made against you in this, but you do agree with this statement that you were replaced by Dragan Djuric who was a Serb extremist. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, skip forward a couple pages probably. There's a heading "public security station." And the first paragraph under that heading starts with the words: "This organ has 70 employees, 48 policemen..." Et cetera.

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You've found that?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And it states that Milenko Savic is the chief of the SJB police station. Did you know Mr. Savic?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And it states he was an economics graduate and a Serb with 17 years of professional experience who had held a series of leading posts of responsibility in the administrative organ.

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Is that true what I've -- what is stated in this sentence we've just read out together?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You agree with me that -- well, do you think that Mr. Savic was a decent professional police chief?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You were pushed out in February, allegedly, for not being amongst the most extreme Serb leadership in Prnjavor. What happened to Mr. Savic, say, in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, he, too, faced problems. I don't know at which point exactly, but he was facing problems with the same structures as I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And one of his problems was that he wasn't a member of the SDS. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: This may have been the case, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, you know that he was not a member of the SDS. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it wasn't that important. What mattered more was Mr. Savic was an old hand. Maybe he refused change. So this can be seen in two ways. I'm not really sure that that was the reason. Based on this example, you can't --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Go ahead and finish.

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: If you look at this example, I'm not sure that he was eliminated from power simply because he was not a member of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You agree that could have been a factor?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: I do agree. This may have been one of the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I think you're right that it was because in part he was old school and didn't agree with all the changes which may have been coming. Isn't it correct that the SDS leadership felt that it could not depend on him to push their programme in Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: At the time the SDS platform was not that extremist. There were still people around who were conscious of the need for a democratic society. It was only later that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me stop you. You've just agreed with me that this document is correct and the statements in here are correct, that extreme SDS Serbs, extremist leaders were taking over or were leading the Serb party at this time. You'd explained that's why you were replaced. Right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The reason he was replaced, because he was not sufficiently extreme; he would not carry out orders that were illegal. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I would ask at this time that the witness be permitted to answer the question and not interrupted. It's being asked a second time, and this time I hope he'll be allowed to answer it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say either of these two with sure and certain knowledge. I can't say for sure that this was the reason. Despite the fact that I had been eliminated, chucked out of the party, there were still people who could effect future change and who refused to allow extremism to spread. I, too, was persistent in my efforts. Naturally, I was the president of the party, after all. So in answer to your question, I'm not certain about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You're not certain, but you the president of the party were kicked out. You're certain about that?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So it's highly plausible, you'll grant me, that he could have been pushed out for the same reasons, the reasons I've suggested to you, that he was not --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think that's a completely fair question. He said he doesn't know exactly, but based on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's the fourth time it's been asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, it's a different question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So he can say for the fourth time that he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Answer the question, please. It is different. It's being put to him in a different manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You can answer the question, sir, if you remember. Is it not entirely plausible based on what you know that the reason that Mr. Savic was removed from his position as chief of police is because the SDS felt that it could not count on him or depend on him to carry out orders in the coming period, their plan for the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now you have changed it in a way that Mr. Ackerman would be right in objecting to because you have rephrased it exactly the way you had phrased it before when he had given you an answer. The question that I allowed you to --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I can repeat the question exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's highly plausible --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will grant me that he could have been pushed out for the same reasons, the reasons that I've suggested to you, and then you were interrupted. Basically it's being put to you that both you and Mr. Savic were pushed off for basically the same reasons, that you did not fit in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure that it was for the same reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The question is that it's plausible that it was.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The question is not that you were a hundred per cent sure, but it makes sense based on what happened to you. It makes sense, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, how many times did he have to answer the same question over and over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is the last time, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So this time when he says he's not sure, that'll be the end?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you for suggesting the answer, Mr. Ackerman, but the question is different. He keeps saying he's not sure exactly what happened, that's not the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The question is not different. He keeps saying is it plausible, it's plausible isn't it? And he keeps saying I don't know. How many times do we have to do this. We can stay here all day and ask the same question over and over and he can give the same answer over and over. Mr. Nicholls is not going to be happy until he gets the answer he wants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You think Mr. Nicholls is going to get the answer he wants?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He says I'm not sure it was for the same reason. That's not answering the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What makes you unsure, Mr. Vidic? What makes you unsure? Because at a certain point in time - look at me - at a certain point in time the situation changed. You got pushed off. He got pushed off. Others got pushed off. The situation changed. Why did it change.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really hesitate to interrupt but there's really no foundation for this -- for these questions. Because there's not showing that he knows from the people who pushed Savic out why it was they pushed Savic out. If he hadn't talked to those people and learned from them why they pushed Savic out, how could he possibly give an answer here that's of any value to anyone?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, the way the witness answered the question before shows that he does know or, at least, he knows more than he has told us. When he was pushed to answer whether not being a member of the SDS could have been one of the factors, he said yes, but he hadn't said it before. It was only when he -- and then he gave us to understand that there may have been other reasons one of which was belonging to this -- sort of the old school. I think the witness knows more than he has told us, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If we want him to guess, let's just ask him for his guess and let him guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't want him to guess. I want him to answer the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I can give the foundation very simply. This was a small community. We've gone through this before. This man was president of the SDS. He was involved in the power struggle in the SDS --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's not argue in front of the witness, Mr. Nicholls. Rather, I insist on my own question. At a certain point in time, things changed. Why did things change, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After Savic, there was another man who was not a member of the SDS either who assumed the same position that Savic had held. Therefore, I don't think that really mattered. Perhaps what mattered is that he had been good with me. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, Mr. Nicholls, he's your witness now. But let's move now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me ask you if you agree with this statement: Up to April 1992, and we're breaking at noon, Your Honour, is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You said before. So I'm not sure whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I need two minutes to get to the President's Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Up to April 1992, there was no ethnic cleansing in Prnjavor. In my view, it started officially when the war started, and that is in 1992. Everybody knows this and so do I. But this did not happen in Prnjavor before April --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What are you reading from, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is from a section of the transcript, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, they just went ballistic if I ever did anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That is completely not true. He put to so many witnesses: "Would you agree with the statement that Banja Luka became an ethnic ghetto for non-Serbs" or something like that. He knows exactly what I'm doing is proper. It's the same thing that he's been allowed to do. I'm not identifying where this came from or what it's about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He's identifying that it's testimony. He's reading the exact words of the testimony. Ms. Korner objected over and over and you --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That is simply a completely misleading statement by Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I see nothing irregular about this. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Up to April 1992, there was no ethnic cleansing in Prnjavor. In my view, it started officially when the war started, and that is in 1992. Everybody knows this, and so do I. But this did not happen in Prnjavor before April, or rather, I think it was May, June, July when the problem in Lisnje happened. But there wasn't any ethnic cleansing up to that time. There was tension, but there was not ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall we stop here, and he will think about the question and give us an answer when we resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. 25 minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Nicholls. Mr. Vidic, do you need me to repeat the question to you or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to read out to you what I have here. "Up to April 1992, there was no ethnic cleansing in Prnjavor. In my view, it started officially when the war started, and that is in 1992. Everybody knows this, and so do I. But this did not happen in Prnjavor before April, or rather, I think it was May, June, July when the problem in Lisnje happened. But there wasn't any ethnic cleansing up to that time. There was tension, but there was not ethnic cleansing." And we stopped here so that you could have a coffee and we could attend to our duties as well. Doesn't mean to say that we did not have a coffee. Mr. Nicholls, your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, you were in Prnjavor at that time. You've heard that statement which the Judge has read out to you again. Do you agree that that is an accurate statement of the situation in Prnjavor during the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are a number of things --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think there are eight questions, I counted them, in that one phrase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are not correct in your counting. There has perhaps half.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have no objection to the witness answering the way it's phrased if he believes he can. But if he wants to answer it in separate parts, he can do that, too. I don't want to be here all day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vidic, do you think you need to take that statement bit by bit, or can you give us a straight answer taking it as it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Part by part, bit by bit, because it's quite lengthy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I can break this down. It will take a little longer, but it's okay because we've got all of today and tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Was there ethnic cleansing in Prnjavor before April 1992?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: No. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you agree with this statement insofar as that goes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It started officially when the war started, and that is in 1992. Do you agree with that statement, that sentence?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Partially, but I would say no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What do you partially agree with in that statement?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: The question is whether a legal legitimate intervention by the police against civilians who are armed or are disturbing public law and order, whether that would constitute ethnic cleansing. I am not sure that at that time there were any drastic examples --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop, stop. You are an educated man with a university education. I take it well read, and certainly not the kind of person who for the first time is hearing the phrase "ethnic cleansing." I hope you're not. It just doesn't tune in, at least in my mind, how someone like you with your education can get confused with a legal, legitimate intervention by the police against civilians who are armed or are disturbing public law and order can in any way that you may volunteer to describe to us become or constitute ethnic cleansing. That's unless you have a very perverted view of what ethnic cleansing is all about. And I'm being very blunt with you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Endangering civilians and the persecution of civilians, this is what I would call ethnic cleansing and violating their human rights and liberties. Where there is such pressure on civilians, I would refer to that as ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, do you agree that that took place in Prnjavor Municipality, what you just described, during the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: I don't know about the municipality of Prijedor, but I do believe, I do say that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think I got a translation error. I said Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The transcript says Prnjavor. I wouldn't know what the interpretation --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We're only talking about Prnjavor now. Answer the question, please. I'm sorry, I heard Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: At that time, the situation was quite specific. The question is whether the all the ethnic cleansing was conducted by the local authorities. You could not say that because there was a lot of chaos --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That was not the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, I think I have to go back to the core of this issue because the witness says within the context of ethnic cleansing, trying to define it, how he understands it, and then you follow up with questions, he says endangering civilians and the persecution of civilians, that is what I would call ethnic cleansing, and violating their human rights and liberties. We have ethnic -- two words, "ethnic" and "cleansing" combined together in one context. What ethnic group are we talking about here with reference to Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And what do you understand by cleansing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The pressure on them to move out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right it's much more clear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unlawful arrests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it you're being very honest with the Trial Chamber. Now it's clear. It has been put within the context of both ethnicity and also an operation of cleansing. Moving on, so Mr. Nicholls, now you can put your questions, and they will be more answerable, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, having told the Chamber your understanding of that term "ethnic cleansing," did that occur in the Municipality of Prnjavor during the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that occurred in Lisnje village. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to, I'm sorry, briefly go back...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I see the transcript says "no audible response." It could well be -- can I ask you, Mr. Vidic, to come nearer to the microphones, or perhaps usher could position the microphones in a way that they can receive.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, I want you to be comfortable. We're recording everything said here today; that's why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the thing is that your answer, which I heard from here, was not heard by the interpreters. So the question was you were first asked: "Ethnic cleansing, did that occur in the Municipality of Prnjavor during the summer of 1992?" You said yes. And then you were further asked: "And that occurred in Lisnje village, correct?" I heard you say yes, but the interpreters did not hear you. Do you confirm that you said yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we could go back to P1785, the document you were looking at earlier, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I apologise. If we could go back to P1785.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it still on the ELMO? Yes, it's still on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Page 4 of the B/C/S, page 3 -- although it's not marked, page 3 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Before we get to this, sir, were you ever a member - you may have answered this; if you did, I apologise - of the Prnjavor municipal crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Who was the president of that crisis staff when it was in existence?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Who was president -- sorry?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Who was the president of the municipality before the crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Nemanja Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Does that help your memory at all as to who was president of the crisis staff, too? If it doesn't, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I assume that Mr. Nemanja Vasic was, but it was a long time ago, so I don't really remember whether he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. If you look at page 4, it's on the -- to your right. It's not in the binder. You've got it. The top paragraph, if I've got it correctly, should start with: "The executive committee of the municipal assembly comprises eight members." Is that right, what you have in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. It then states as follows: "Radivoje Radivojevic is chairman." Now, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Radivoje Radivojevic. I have to make this correction. Yes, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Was he a qualified engineer, this man?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did he belong to an extreme faction?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. He was more of a professional, professional when it came to municipal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He was a member of the crisis staff, was he not, the municipal crisis staff in Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You don't recall him being thrown out of his position the way you were and the way chief Savic was, do you?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me ask you --

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: As far as he's concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me ask you to speak up a bit. Some of these questions you're answering very quietly. That's fine, but we just need to make sure that the interpreters can hear you. Do you believe -- we can skip the phrase that he was very self-seeking. To your knowledge, was he one of the people who you've talked about who were involved in smuggling arms?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you know he wasn't, or you don't know whether he was or not?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: It's a difficult question. As far as I know, however, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I've got to ask: What's difficult about that question? It seems pretty simple and straightforward to me. What did you mean when you said that was a difficult question?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: It may be true that you or somebody else know that he smuggled weapons. But I don't know about that. I do not know that he did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I'm just curious, have you seen this gentleman recently or spoken with him?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: I did not see him. I haven't seen him in over a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Have you talked to him in over a year -- in the last year on the telephone?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I do know that some time ago, perhaps a year ago or so, we met about a project for his apartment. He wanted to buy an apartment, and I do projects of apartments for a company. And that was the only issue. His daughter came, and she also wanted to know about the apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's all right. Thank you. Now, if you go to page 3, it will be towards, I think, the bottom of the page. I'm sorry, I've got that wrong. Page 2 at the top of the page. I'm sorry. It's also page 2 in English. We see "Evaluation of political parties." Do you see that heading? It would be at the top of page 2 in your language.

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It begins by talking about how the SDS won a majority, and we've talked about that. Later on in that same paragraph it states: "The SDS leadership gathered around Dragan Djuric, Veljko Milankovic, Radivoje Radivojevic, and Nemanja Vasic, and some others, publicly advocate the formation of Chetnik black Trojka units. Have you read that part?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, based on your knowledge of being former president of the SDS there, were these men, Dragan Djuric, Veljko Milankovic, Radivojevic, and Mr. Vasic people who, as it states here, were of the same political mind who gathered together?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: This would be too strong a qualification. That is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I'll ask an open-ended question. You describe the relationship between these men I've just asked you about. What was it like in March, April, May 1992 in Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nemanja Vasic and Mr. Radivoje Radivojevic were on good terms. One was the president of the municipality, and the other one was the chairman of the executive board. Veljko Milankovic, I know that they did not like him, and he caused a great deal of problems for them. But they did not have any options or they did not have any courage since they did not have police under their control at that time, and they were just setting up the civilian authorities. But I know that Mr. Veljko Milankovic was causing them trouble. And I know that they were not on good terms with him. But they sometimes would meet in the same place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What would they meet with Veljko Milankovic to talk about, even if their relationship was as you characterise it?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Veljko Milankovic frequented the SDS premises, or actually he went there when they would meet, and he usurped the proceedings, and he would disrupt their work. But I don't know whether they put him on the board because they were forced to do so. But I do know that while I was the president, I insisted on Veljko Milankovic, who was a person like that and who did not represent any local community, that he could not be a member of the SDS. I had problems because of that, but I insisted on that point. While I was there, he did not have the power to decide. However, when they came on board, I know that they tried to avoid him. But he was active there, too. This is as much as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And you weren't at those meetings, so you don't know exactly what was discussed between these men. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: No. At that time, I did not attend any meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You'd already been replaced?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there seems to be a fairly significant transcript problem. 69/6, page 69, line 6, "they did not have any courage" which I thought was strange when I heard it. I'm told that what he said was "since they belonged to the civil authorities, they did not have any police under their control at the time." I don't think the "did not have any courage" appeared there at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think he said something about the police under their control earlier, but I can ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we need to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Wait a minute, I'm told I'm wrong about that, too. He did say it about the courage, but the first part where he said they belonged to the civil authorities. I don't know. It's very confusing to me at this point to me even.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go through it. Mr. Vidic, sometime back you were asked this question: "All right. I'll ask you an open-ended question. You describe the relationship between these men I've just asked you about. What was it like in March, April, May 1992 in Prnjavor?" And this is what we have in the transcript: "Mr. Nemanja Vasic and Mr. Radivoje Radivojevic were on good terms. One was the president of the municipality and the other one was the chairman of the executive board. Veljko Milankovic, I know, that they did not like him, and he caused a great deal of problems for them. But they did not have any options and they didn't" - this is where the problem starts - "but they did not have any options or they did not have any courage since they did not have police under their control at the time and they were just setting up the civilian authorities." Does it make sense to you, or do you want to correct anything? It's a question of transcript, it's not a question of whether you have been clear or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's how it was. They did not have -- yes, yes. I abide by what I have just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it okay, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I guess so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's take it up, then, from where we had left it before. And yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I've lost whichever question I may have asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's okay. I'll help you. I'll help you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And you weren't at those meetings so you don't know exactly what was discussed between these men. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: No, at the time I did not attend any meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You had already been replaced? And then Mr. Ackerman interjected. And this was all being said, questioned and answered in relation to Milankovic and his relationship inside the group.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: My point is, sir, you've described this relationship. You don't really know what these men may have said to each other during their meetings because you weren't present. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: One thing - and going through all of this again of this correction - surprised me you said they didn't have any police. What about chief of the local police there, Mr. Savic? Didn't he, in fact, later on take part in arresting them?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. But not then when the president of the municipality or the civilian authorities wanted it, when there is a certain consensus, when you get the support of the higher superior ranks of the -- actually superior organs of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. So there needed to be a consensus in the superior organs of the police that it was necessary to arrest Mr. Milankovic? Is that what you're saying? I think that's what you just said, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, who were the superior organs of the police who at that time - we're talking about March, April - did not think it was yet ripe to arrest Mr. Milankovic?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Under the ministry of police, which was centralised, down to the ministry of police --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, sir, you're whispering, at least that's what it sounds like to me. If you could just speak a little bit louder.

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Police had the chain of command for certain things, and it was under the ministry of police. The AR Krajina could not influence the police, only the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina which passed its constitution and laws on the Ministry of the Interior could do that. They set up the whole structure, and they appointed people at the higher levels of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And so you're saying that the people at the highest level of the police had not reached a consensus or did not want Veljko Milankovic arrested. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: No. That's not what I mean. The events happened quite fast. Veljko Milankovic was not the only person causing trouble. There were other similar groups, and trying to enter the fray with such groups was a dangerous thing at the time. And that is why there had to be collaboration with the superior organs and throughout the whole organisation in such actions because it was not a question of just this one man, Veljko Milankovic, but of all the people that he had, his men, who were all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you look at P82, please. Now, what I'd like you to do, you can skip the cover letter which is signed "Stojan Zupljanin" and go to the report on the activity of the armed groups of the centre's territory. Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I've got just a few questions about this, but I'd like you if you could to just read from the report pages 1, 2, and 3. Sorry, that will take a moment, but I'm going to ask you some questions about it. I want to make sure you've read it.

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: My apologies. The paragraphs, not the pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, the first three pages which describe the activities of Veljko Milankovic and his group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: While he reads, what's your question going to be? Because knowing that, I would see whether it's necessary for the witness to read first three pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, and I wouldn't want --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then get Mr. Ackerman stand up, object, and we have to go straight to the first sentence. So let's see what's cooking.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I wouldn't want to go line by line, but what I wanted to see if he agrees, if he remembers these incidents that are described here, these activities by Milankovic's group, and the individuals involved on the scale of the problem in Prnjavor. I thought it might be easier if he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Maybe you are right. So Mr. Vidic, go ahead, read the three pages. And when you are ready, let me know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I've finished the first three pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And I hope --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would suggest that you be very articulate about your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I will try to be, Your Honour, and try not to cause Mr. Ackerman any concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Having read that document, has that helped you in any way to refresh your memory about the activities of Veljko Milankovic and his men in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, it has.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you agree that it was in July or thereabouts in 1991 that this group led by Milankovic came to Prnjavor from Knin? You correct me if it's a different time.

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not sure about the month, but it was in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: They came -- well, first of all, Veljko Milankovic was well known in Prnjavor before the war, before these ethnic tensions. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He was known as a notorious criminal?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He went to Knin for training, military training?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Who sent him to Knin for that training?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: At that time, they requested volunteers from Knin, the municipal authorities in Knin requested humanitarian aid. They requested people to come over. People started reporting. He owned a bus. In fact, he owned a private company. They ran buses, and he used this bus to collect people and drive them to Knin. That's what I know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Back up a second. You just agreed with me that Veljko Milankovic went to Knin for military training. He was not just running some kind of taxi service. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: No, no. He left, that's at least what I learned, only to provide taxi service. However, once he reached Knin, he reported and stayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And he received --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question is, still I don't know how many lines later, we're still pretty much confused. Mr. Vidic, Mr. Nicholls asked you a question some time back. He said, referring to Milankovic, he went to Knin for training, military training. And you said yes. That was your answer. Then he asked you, who sent him to Knin for that training? And you have been telling us about buses, taxis, transporting people. Could you please now tell us whether you know who sent him to Knin for that military training? Because that's what we want to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, he answered that. He said there was a volunteer request, and he was a volunteer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, he hasn't answered it in any way, Mr. Ackerman. I'm not stupid, Mr. Ackerman. Read it all from beginning to end, and you will see that he has been trying to answer everything except that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I respectfully disagree. Lines 8 through 12 are a pretty clear answer to that question. They called for volunteers, and he volunteered and went and took his bus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Military training.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He answered it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, it's not --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He's not playing around it, he answered it. Look at lines 8 through 12, Judge. I think you just didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Mr. Ackerman, it's completely different. Let's go through it bit by bit if you want. "Who sent him to Knin for that training?" And he said: "At that time, they requested volunteers from Knin. The municipal authorities in Knin requested humanitarian aid." And that's what he responded to, according to the witness. He had a bus, and he started using that bus by taking people to Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think what he said was among the things they requested was humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question before was who sent him to Knin for that training, the military training? And that's the answer I want to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think his answer is pretty clear. Nobody did, he went as a volunteer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's enough, Mr. Ackerman. You have acknowledged already that Milankovic went or undertook military training in Knin. Who sent him to Knin for the military training? Or who was instrumental in that military training being given to Milankovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were various agitators who were taking people to Krajina. Many of them even boasted about this or that person. Whether it was someone there leading the whole thing, that's one thing that I was not aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand your answer completely.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, I don't understand your answer completely. Many of them boasted about this or that person. What do you mean there? I'm just trying to ask you who was it who sent Veljko Milankovic to Knin for military training? And you're talking about people boasting about this or that person. Could you be a little more specific, please.

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: I do not know who took Veljko Milankovic to Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You do know, don't you, that he and his unit were involved in the takeover of the Kozara transmitter?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That was after he returned from Knin, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: I think so. I don't know. Perhaps if I could have my memory refreshed. But yes, I think so. Yes. I don't know. I can't answer your question with precision, but yes, after all, yes. Yes, later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When Milankovic returned to Prnjavor, did he have about 30 armed persons with him? Is that an accurate -- reasonably accurate figure, from your knowledge of how many people were operating in his group in Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were they well armed with pistols, automatic weapons, bazookas, and grenades?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I don't want to go through all of this line by line. But is it true that they used these weapons to harass, intimidate, threaten the population -- or just say people in Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Is it true that on main roads, they set up checkpoints and they conducted illegal searches of cars and that they actually committed thefts from citizens?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Is it true that individually and as a group, they provoked and harassed the Muslim population with the aim of precipitating interethnic conflict -- interethnic fighting? Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Not Muslims only. They mistreated everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think you're right about that. But isn't it true that they were particularly threatening and focussed on the Muslim or Bosniak population in Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: It was more against the Muslims than anyone else. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We've agreed that there was ethnic cleansing in Lisnje in the summer of 1992. Milankovic was involved in that, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And those were Bosniaks who were driven out during that particular campaign. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you've told us, and you told Mr. Ackerman -- you explained at some length how when the multiparty elections occurred and when these new democratic institutions were being set up, your idea was to have a sort of pluralistic multiethnic party, but that that didn't happen. Right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And although you were a member of the SDS and the SDS president, you were pushed out of office?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that was by the more -- I'll use the word nationalistic elements of the SDS in Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: It was more that they didn't really understand democracy than being obsessed by hate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I didn't say "obsessed by hate." But they certainly were not interested in your ideas about a multiethnic party?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And in fact, has it never occurred to you that it would have been useful for that SDS leadership in Prnjavor to have Veljko Milankovic causing these disruptions and fear in the Bosniak population? Has that ever occurred to you, that he was useful to the SDS leadership?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: There's a dilemma there. What I understood was that other, unknown people had influence on him. What I'm confused by, however, is the hostility between him on the one hand and the municipal bodies on the other. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Why don't you try to answer that question again. Start over, because you sort of faded out. Hasn't it ever occurred to you -- isn't it true that Veljko Milankovic's activities after he returned from Knin were useful and positive for the SDS party and leadership?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: You can't say that. As far as I was aware, and I did talk to people at that time, you know, the multiethnic assembly was still operating with Muslims, Croats, and other parties in it. It was still operating. The municipality, there was -- the feeling was more fear of unrest than an ambition to deter unrest in the municipality. Also the president, the way I saw it, regardless of their relationship. It's just that they simply failed to understand my idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not talking about your ideas right now. I'll try it this way. Veljko Milankovic's unit, the Wolves, were well armed and ruthless. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: They saw themselves as Serb heroes?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: There were others who saw them as Serb heroes?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That included some of the top SDS leadership and some of the SDS leadership in Prnjavor. Stop. That included some members of the SDS leadership in Prnjavor. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: I don't know about those particular relations. I really can't say anything about anyone there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I'll move on in a minute. But something you said earlier, I think it has gone off the screen, was that nobody knew, you were saying, who had influence over Veljko Milankovic. The takeover of the Kozara tower was viewed as a very positive development by the Krajina leadership, wasn't it? He was, in fact, congratulated by Dr. Vukic and Grahovac. Do you remember reading that, for this Kozara takeover?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: It may very well have been the case. I'm not certain about it, but at one point in time, there was a person who was always there in touch with Grahovac. That's precisely what some other people among us did not like. So we moved for a decision within Krajina to express displeasure about that. This was no authentic expression of Krajina. I think this was a misuse, a case of misuse of that particular unit. There was no need for anything like that. Who was it to place another extra channel on the repeater itself? This would have been no problem at all. It was something perfectly legal, after all. I don't think there was a real reason to use force there, least of all for this force to be used on behalf of Krajina. As far as I remember, I became involved in this as well as other people from this area. We couldn't come to terms with the fact that certain groups were boasting about being part of Krajina, or rather the assembly of Krajina at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You said a minute ago there was a person.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You said a moment ago there was a person who was always there in touch with Grahovac. Who's that person? Who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Miro Mladjenovic. May I just be allowed to say something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin had a run-in with Mr. Mladjenovic in connection with these very things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were you present at this run-in?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Not for the biggest run-in, but later at a session that occurred later, I heard about this very strong animosity, and I heard about the reasons for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Are you --

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: Miro Mladjenovic, and the reporter, he was a reporter himself, took pictures, photographs, of Veljko Milankovic, or rather, of his men. And they came to Krajina before we realised what was going on. And that is why later, we took a stand on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just to be clear, what period are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE VIDIC
utterances.text: It is the period in 1991, the fall of 1991, as far as I can remember, after the summer. In fact, just after the end of summer, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next thing I was going to do involves playing an audiotape and a recording. If it's acceptable to the Chamber, I'd rather just start off with that tomorrow rather than start and begin questions on it and not finish. I can say that I will definitely finish tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it okay with you, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is okay with me. Can I know what video it is that's going to be used tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's an audiotape, and the transcript has been disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is it on the list of exhibits that you've given us?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Doesn't have an exhibit number yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think I know what it is, Your Honour. It's the 0323 -- one of those two 0323 documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Blagojevic is sitting tomorrow? It's still sitting. It's not cancelled by any chance? So there is no way we can move to the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm now so utterly confused by this timetable. Tomorrow is the afternoon, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Wednesday is the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thursday is the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Friday is the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Make eminent common sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're telling me, Ms. Korner. Yes, Mr. Vidic, we have to stop here because tomorrow we're starting a new chapter, and I don't think we can finish that in the few minutes that we have left. So take a rest, and you will come here again tomorrow afternoon starting at 2.15. And hopefully we will finish with you tomorrow and you would be able to go back home. Madam Usher will now escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that's it. We stand adjourned until tomorrow at 2.15. I think it's the same courtroom, Courtroom II. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 2nd day of December, 2003, at 2.15 p.m. 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.35 p.m.,
